A creature who is {@b three-quarters flanked} suffers a -5 penalty to AC and Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} against sources within 5 feet of it. A creature is three-quarters flanked if it is at least three-quarters surrounded, either to a side, above, or below.

Alternatively, you can have players add a +2, +3, or +5 bonus to their {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack rolls} against creatures who are one-quarter, half, or three-quarters flanked, respectively, by them. Additionally, if you use the Saving Throws Checks variant, you can instead have them add a +2, +3, or +5 bonus to their Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} checks against creatures who are one-quarter, half, or three-quarters flanked, respectively, by them.

A creature who has a reach of greater than 5 feet gains the benefit of flanking against a creature while within melee range, but does not contribute towards flanking unless they are within 5 feet of the target.

{@b {@i Flanking on Squares.}} On a square grid, a Small or Medium creature takes up one square, and has eight squares surrounding it within 5 feet. When two or three of those squares are occupied by hostile creatures, that creature is considered one-quarter flanked by those creatures. When four or five of those squares are occupied by hostile creatures, that creature is considered half flanked by those creatures. If six or more of those squares are occupied by hostile creatures, that creature is instead considered three-quarters flanked.

{@b {@i Flanking on Hexes.}} On a hex grid, a Small or Medium creature takes up one hex, and has six hexes surrounding it within 5 feet. When two of those squares are occupied by hostile creatures, that creature is considered one-quarter flanked by those creatures. When three or four of those squares are occupied by hostile creatures, that creature is considered half flanked by those creatures. If five or six of those hexes are occupied by hostile creatures, that creature is instead considered three-quarters flanked.

Alternatively, you can run the simpler ruleset for flanking found in the DMG, that offers {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} instead of flat bonuses. That ruleset works alongside Advanced {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb} as well.

entries.name: Standing from Prone while Flanked
entries: When a creature attempts to stand from prone while flanked, it can choose to make a Strength ({@skill Athletics|sw5e-phb}) or Dexterity ({@skill Acrobatics|sw5e-phb}) check (DC = 10 + its penalty from flanking). On a success, the creature stands and can move to an unoccupied space within 5 feet of it without provoking {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attacks}. On a failure, the creature remains prone and loses the movement it would have used to stand.

data.name: Force Alignment
entries: TThe Force is manifested by two powerful and opposing aspects: the Ashla and the Bogan, more commonly known as the light side and the dark. As force-wielding characters evolve throughout the game, they can gravitate towards one side or the other (or neither, should they choose), resulting in physical manifestations and boons.

entries.name: Alignment Score
entries: How much a character embodies an aspect of the Force is calculated using their Alignment Score. The Alignment Score is an ever-shifting value falling between Light 100 to Dark 100. Characters gain an Alignment Score by gaining Light/Dark Points, as determined by their actions.

entries.name: Gaining Light/Dark Points
entries: When a character performs an act associated with one side of the Force, they gain points accordingly. Players can gain Light Points through a multitude of actions:

items: The first time you cast a light side {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} of 1st-level or higher, you gain Light Points equal to the power's level. Subsequent castings of that power earn you 1 Light Point.
Committing selfless acts, such as deliberately saving others at the expense of yourself, can earn you 1 or more Light Points.
Other benevolent acts, as determined by your GM, can earn you 1 or more Light Points.

entries: Consequently, players can also gain Dark Points through various actions:

items: The first time you cast a dark side {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} of 1st-level or higher you gain Dark Points equal to the power's level. Subsequent castings of that power earn you 1 Dark Point.
Committing truly heinous acts, such as harming or murdering an innocent, can earn you 1 or more Dark Points.
Other evil acts, as determined by your GM, can earn you 1 or more Dark Points.

entries: If a character has a score and performs an opposing act, instead of gaining points towards the other aspect of the Force, they lose them from their current score. For instance, if a player has 5 Light Points, and casts a dark side power of 4th level, they would have their Light Points reduced to 1. If the player instead casts a dark side power of 7th level, their score would shift to Dark 2.

entries.name: Alignment Tiers
entries: As you earn Light/Dark Points, you reach certain tiers of Alignment Score that manifest themselves in varying ways. If you ever fall below the Light/Dark Points threshold for a Major tier, you immediately lose that tier's benefits. You regain the benefits when you meet the criteria again. Minor tier effects are permanent unless another similar effect occurs.

entries.name: Minor Benevolence/Corruption
entries: At certain tiers of Light/Dark Points, you risk manifesting Minor Traits, as shown in the Force Alignment table. When you would earn a Minor Trait, you must first make a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} (Charisma for Benevolence, Wisdom for Corruption), the DC of which varies depending on the tier of the Minor Trait, as shown in the Minor Benevolence/Corruption Save DC table below. On a failed save, you must roll on a Minor Benevolence/Corruption tables, depending on the tier of the Minor Benevolence/Corruption. You can choose to fail this {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, if you wish.

Your body is less likely to scar or show lasting signs of injury.
Your voice becomes slightly more eloquent.
Tame animals seem less uneasy around you.
Your eyes become more stark and vibrant.
Any existing scars on your body fade, and wounds never scar or fester.
Your voice gains a pleasant, melodic speaking cadence.
Your hair gains subtle highlights of gold or silver that occasionally reflect light.
Your eyes gain flecks of an unusual, complimenting color, such as amber or emerald.
Your skin always has a healthy tone.
You never suffer from minor illnesses, always appearing to be the pinnacle of health.
Wild animals become significantly less prone to attacking you.
Your eyes permanently take on an unusual, complimenting color, such as green becoming bright emerald.
Your voice has a naturally calming quality that puts others at easy.
You seem all but immune to naturally occurring illnesses.
Your hair takes on visible streaks of gold or silver.
Your hair begins to wither and fall out.
Your eyes permanently gain a faint glow.
You exude a calming presence that brings a slight feeling of peace to those around you.
Withered or sickly plants seem to liven in your presence.
You appear 1d10 years more youthful than you actually are. This does not change your actual life span.
Your eyes turn a pale yellow during moments of anger.
Your hair starts to lose its color, with gray streaks appearing throughout it.
Your eyes turn a luminous, sulfuric yellow with fiery red rims around the irises during moments of anger.
Any scars on your body become more noticeable, and your wounds become more pronounced.
Your voice lowers in pitch and becomes raspier.
Your eyes permanently turn a luminous, sulfuric yellow with fiery red rings around the irises.
Your skin begins to lose its pigmentation, becoming pale and mottled.
Your veins become increasingly visible across your entire body, as if they are sticking out.
Your hair loses its color entirely, turning a stark white.
Your eyes permanently turn a luminous, dark orange with fiery red rings around the irises.
Your skin loses its pigmentation, turning nearly stark white, while your veins become even more accentuated.
Your nails and claws begin to wither and grow longer, turning a vile yellow color.
Your hair begins to wither and fall out.
Your eyes permanently turn a luminous, blood red with fiery red rings around the irises.
You appear physically devoid of emotions. Your feelings never project outwards.
You develop a sickly, uncontrollable cough.
You appear 1d10 year older than you actually are. This does not change your actual life span.

entries.name: Major Benevolence
entries: At certain tiers of Light Points, as shown in the Force Alignment table, you manifest a Major Benevolence.

entries.name: Tier I
entries: When you or an ally within 30 feet of you makes a Charisma ({@skill Persuasion|sw5e-phb}) check to attempt to calm a creature or bring peace/alliance, you may spend a force point to add 1d4 to the result of the roll.

entries.name: Tier II
entries: When a friendly creature other than you within 30 feet that you can see fails a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} against being {@condition Frightened|sw5e-phb|frightened}, you can spend 1 force point to have them reroll the die. They must use the new roll.

entries.name: Tier III
entries: When an ally within 30 feet of you rolls a 1 on the {@dice d20} for an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} or {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, you can spend 1 force point to let the ally reroll the die. They must use the new roll.

entries.name: Tier IV
entries: Casting light side {@book force powers|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} of 1st level or higher costs 1 fewer force point, but casting {@book dark side powers|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} of 1st level or higher costs 1 more.

entries.name: Luminous Being (Tier V)
entries: You have become a physical manifestation of the light side of the Force, gaining one of the following boons. Your GM can choose the boon for you, or roll a die to determine it randomly.
{@b {@i Lightbringer.}} Your maximum force points increases by 10.

{@b {@i Protection.}} When a friendly creature other than you within 30 feet that you can see takes damage from any source, you can reduce that damage to 0. Once you've used this boon, you can't use it again until you finish a short or {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}.
{@b {@i Immutable Defense.}} The damage resistances of friendly creatures other than you within 30 feet of you cannot be ignored.

{@b {@i Quick Casting.}} Choose one light side {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} you know of 1st through 3rd level that has a casting time of 1 action. That power's casting time is now 1 {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} for you.

{@b {@i Lay On Hands.}} You can use a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} and touch a friendly creature other than yourself, causing them to recover a number of {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} equal to half their hit point maximum. Once you've used this boon, you can't use it again until you finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}.

{@b {@i Healer.}} If a friendly creature within 30 feet of you regains {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} at the end of a {@variantrule Short Rest|sw5e-phb|short rest} by spending one or more Hit Dice, that creature regains additional {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} equal to your Wisdom modifier.

entries.name: Major Corruption
entries: At certain tiers of Dark Points, as shown in the Force Alignment table, you manifest a Major Corruption.

entries.name: Tier I
entries: You have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on Charisma ({@skill Intimidation|sw5e-phb}) checks and {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on Wisdom ({@skill Insight|sw5e-phb}) checks made against creatures with a higher Wisdom score than you.

entries.name: Tier II
entries: You have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} against being {@condition Frightened|sw5e-phb|frightened}, and {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} against being {@condition Charmed|sw5e-phb|charmed}.

entries.name: Tier III
entries: You have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} made against dark side {@book force powers|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers}. Additionally, when you receive healing from light side {@book force powers|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers}, you only regain half the amount of {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}.

entries.name: Tier IV
entries: Casting dark side {@book force powers|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} of 1st level or higher costs 1 fewer force point, but casting {@book light side powers|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} of 1st level or higher costs 1 more.

entries.name: Dark Entity (Tier V)
entries: You have become a physical manifestation of the dark side of the Force, gaining one of the following boons. Your GM can choose the boon for you, or roll a die to determine it randomly.
{@b {@i Deathbringer.}} Your maximum force points increases by 10.

{@b {@i Invincibility.}} When you take damage from any source, you can reduce that damage to 0. Once you've used this boon, you can't use it again until you finish a short or {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}.
{@b {@i Irresistible Offense.}} You can bypass the damage resistances of any creature.

{@b {@i Quick Casting.}} Choose one dark side {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} you know of 1st through 3rd level that has a casting time of 1 action. That power's casting time is now 1 {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} for you.

{@b {@i Recovery.}} You can use a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} to recover a number of {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} equal to half your hit point maximum. Once you use this boon, you can't use it again until you finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}.
{@b {@i Power Mastery.}} Choose one 1st-level dark side power that you can cast. You can now cast that power at its lowest level without expending force points.

data.name: Force and Tech Prowess
entries: When you fail an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check}, if you added your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} to the check and you did not have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} or {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage}, you can spend 1 force or tech point to reroll the die. You can only use this feature once per {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check}, and you must use the new roll.

data.name: Force-Bond
entries: When two Force-sensitive individuals spend time together, they can develop a powerful connection through the Force. While bonded in such a fashion, the two individuals gain a series of boons, depending on the strength of their bond. However, if the bond is unwilling, the individuals risk corruption by the dark side of the Force.

entries.name: Developing a Bond
entries: When one creature wants to develop a bond with another, they must spend 1 hour meditating, which can be done during a {@variantrule Short Rest|sw5e-phb|short rest},  while within 30 feet of a target that they can see. At the end of this meditation, the target must make a Charisma {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}. The DC of this {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} is equal to the initiator's universal force save DC, and the target of this feature can choose to fail this save. On a failure, the two creature's develop a Force-bond.

entries.name: Valid Targets
entries: Only sentient creatures who can cast {@book force powers|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} of 1st-level or higher can develop a Force-bond, and a creature can only be bonded in such a way to one other creature a time.

entries.name: Strengthening a Bond
entries: In order to strengthen their bond, bond-mates must remain with a certain distance of each other, as shown below in the Bond Distance and DC by Tier table. They must spend one week times the tier they are trying to achieve. For instance, to progress from 1st to 2nd tier takes two weeks, while progressing from 2nd to 3rd takes an additional three weeks. This time does not have to be continuous; bond-mates can spend three days together, two days apart, and then four more days together to achieve 2nd tier.

entries.name: Bond Distance and DC by Tier
Bond Features
entries: At each tier, bond-mates unlock a certain feature. In order to benefit from these features, bond-mates must be within 10 feet of eachother. This distance changes as their bond strengthens, as shown above in the Bond Distance and DC by Tier table.
For instance, at 1st tier, the bond-mates must be within 10 feet of each other to benefit from their bond's features. At 2nd tier, however, they must only be within 30 feet of each other.

entries.name: 1st Tier
entries: Both bond-mates always know precisely where their bond-mate is in relation to them, regardless of whether or not they can see or hear them.

entries.name: 2nd Tier
entries: Both bond-mates can speak with each other as if they were standing within 5 feet, provided they share a language. At 6th tier, this communication becomes telepathic.

entries.name: 3rd Tier
entries: Both bond-mates are constantly under the effects of the {@i sense emotions} {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers}, but they are only able to read each other's emotions. This does not require {@variantrule Concentration|sw5e-phb|concentration} for either bond-mate, and this feature can not be interrupted while both bond-mates are conscious.

entries.name: 4th Tier
entries: As an action on each of their turns, bond-mates can pass items to each other. When a bond-mate uses their action in such a way, the other bond-mate must use their {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to take the item.

entries.name: 5th Tier
entries: Whenever a bond-mate makes an {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} or {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} with {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} due to the other bond-mate taking the {@action Help|sw5e-phb} action, they can reroll one of the dice once.

entries.name: 6th Tier
entries: When a bond-mate casts a {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers}, they can cast it as if they are standing within 5 feet of their bond-mate. If the power requires a target, and that target is not their bond-mate, they must be aware of the target's presence and location in order to target them with this power.

entries.name: 7th Tier
entries: When a bond-mate casts a power of 1st-level or higher that targets only themself, they can also target their bond-mate.

entries.name: 8th Tier
entries: Whenever a bond-mate is reduced to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}, but not killed outright, the other bond-mate can use their {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to cause them to drop to 1 hit point instead.
Once this feature has been used, neither bond-mate can use it again until they both complete a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}.

entries.name: 9th Tier
entries: On their turn, one bond-mate can use their action to give their bond-mate an additional turn. If they do so, the targeted bond-mate immediately takes an additional turn after the current bond-mate's turn.
Once this feature has been used, neither bond-mate can use it again until they both complete a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}.

entries.name: 10th Tier
entries: Whenever a bond-mate takes damage, the other bond-mate can use their {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to grant them resistance to the damage. If they do so, both bond-mates take the same amount of damage. Alternatively, when a bond-mate has {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} restored, they can use their {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to halve the amount of {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}. If they do so, the other bond-mate regains the same number of {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}. These features can be used a number of times equal to the bond-mate's combined Wisdom or Charisma modifiers (their choice, a minimum of once). All expended uses are regained when both bond-mates complete a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}.

entries.name: Breaking a Bond
entries: Sometimes, creatures might want to end their Force-bond, whether the bond was created unbeknownst to them or they no longer wish to share the bond. To do so, one of the creatures must spend 10 minutes meditating on the bond, and then make a Charisma {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}. The DC of this {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} varies, depending on the tier of the bond, as shown above in the Bond Distance and DC by Tier table. On a success, the bond's tier is reduced by 1. If the bond's tier is 1, it is broken. On a failure, the bond's tier is not reduced, and you can't try again for 24 hours.

data.name: Gestalt and Dichotomous Characters
entries: Best suited for smaller parties, gestalt and dichotomous Characters are two separate variant rules that have some conceptual overlap. Gestalt focuses on a character having two classes simultaneously, while, dichotomous focuses on having one class, with two archetypes. If either—or Ashla forbid, both—of these concepts sound intriguing to you, consider the following variant rules.

entries.name: Gestalt Characters
entries: As indicated above, gestalt characters level in two classes simultaneously. They gain all of the proficiencies and features of each class, with following adjustments.

entries.name: Experience Gain
entries: Because a character is leveling in two classes simultaneously, the amount of experience that character should require to gain a level should double. For instance, going from 2nd level to 3rd requires 600 experience points. For a gestalt character, it instead requires 1,200.

entries.name: Hit Points and Hit Dice
entries: If a character chooses two classes with different sized Hit Dice, they should take the average of the two Hit Die sizes (rounded down), and they don't add the Hit Dice together. For instance, if a gestalt character chooses to level in consular, who has a {@dice d6} Hit Die, and guardian, who has a {@dice d10} Hit Die, that character would have a {@dice d8} Hit Die. If the player chooses consular and sentinel, who has a {@dice d8} Hit Die, however, their Hit Die would be a {@dice d6}, since that would be the average of the two Hit Die sizes rounded down.

entries.name: Starting Proficiencies and Equipment
entries: For starting proficiencies and equipment, what you receive varies: {@b {@i Saving Throws.}} You choose the {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} pair offered by either class. You cannot mix-and-match, and you do not get both.
{@b {@i Skills.}} You choose the skills offered by one of your classes. You cannot mix-and-match, and you do not get both.
{@b {@i Weapons, Armor, and Tools.}} You gain the weapons, armor, and tool proficiencies for both classes.
{@b {@i Starting Equipment.}} You gain the starting equipment—or starting wealth—for either class. You cannot mix-and-match, and you do not get both.

entries.name: Ability Score Increases
entries: When a gestalt character reaches 4th, 8th, 12th, 16th, and 19th level, they gain the Ability Score Improvement feature in both classes. At each of these levels, that character should only gain this feature once, instead of twice. Alternatively, you can give them the full +2 Ability Score Improvement from one class, and a feat from the other, as with the ASI and a Feat variant rule.

entries.name: Force- and Tech-Casting
entries: If a character chooses two classes that both have force- or tech-casting, they use the following adjustments:

items: They determine their Max Power Level as if they were multiclassing. If the potential Max Power Level of the two classes combined would exceed 9, however, they instead use the fullcasting Max Power Level progression present on the Multiclass Max Power Level table.
They add the force or tech points from both classes together.
They learn their powers separately by class, as with multiclassing, and those powers are restricted by that class's native Max Power Level regardless of their gestalt Max Power Level.

entries: If a character chooses two classes with opposing casting, they ignore these rules. For instance, if a gestalt character levels as consular and scout, force- and tech-casting are treated separately as determined by their class.

entries.name: Overlapping Features
entries: If two classes receive features that overlap, and aren't otherwise mentioned, it's up to the GM to determine how those features interact.

entries.name: Multiclassing
entries: Gestalt Characters are not suitable for multiclassing.

entries.name: Dichotomous Characters
entries: Instead of your character leveling in two classes simultaneously, you can have your character level in one class, but with two archetypes from that class.

When a character reaches third level, they gain an archetype of their choice for their chosen class. Using this variant, they instead can choose two. At each level within that class that they would gain archetype features, they gain the features for both archetypes. If archetypes offer features that conflict, it's up to the GM to determine how those features interact.
Alternatively, you can have a dichotomous character choose the features of only one archetype at a given level, rather than both, allowing the player to mix and match archetype features.

entries.name: Multiclassing
entries: If a dichotomous character multiclasses, and reaches third level in two or more classes, it's up to the GM to determine whether they gain multiple archetypes in each class, or only in one.

entries.name: Gestalt and Dichotomous
entries: Gestalt and dichotomous characters, since they impact only certain parts of the character generation experience, work seamlessly together. Simply follow the rules associated with gestalt characters, including the restriction on multiclassing, and allow them to choose two archetypes in each class at 3rd level.

data.name: Hunted
entries: In some eras of Star Wars history, forcecasters are a rarity, and are hunted across the galaxy by the likes of Inquisitors, or if they're unlucky, a Dark Lord of the Sith, in an attempt to crush any foreseen threats to their rule. Should you want your {@book forcecasting|sw5e-phb|10|Force- and Tech-casting} players to experience this additional level of drama and suspense, here is an alternate rule to implement: Whenever a player casts a {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers}, others in the Galaxy may detect their presence through ripples in the Force. Each player has a pool of Disturbance Points. This pool of Disturbance Points increases every time a {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} is cast by a number of points equal to the level of the {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} used (at-will powers are treated as Level 0).

After each combat, roll a percentile dice for each player that used a {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers}. If you roll a number equal to or lower than the players Disturbance Pool, they are detected by Jedi Hunters of your determination, who begin to hunt the player they detected.
During each {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}, decrease each player's pool of Disturbance Points by an amount equal to their level.

data.name: Invocation Versatility
entries: With the semi-recent release that added a second level of customization classes that lack them—collectively referred to as invocations, due to their inspiration from the warlock feature of that name—every class now has two levels of customization available to them: their class's invocation feature, and their archetype. Most (all?) of the class's invocation features are hard-locked; that is, once you choose it, you've got it for life. Benevolent GMs might allow players to replace a choice if they found it underwhelming, but others might not. With this variant rule, however, it is encouraged for GMs to allow their player's to rechoose invocations {@i on a case-by-case basis.}

entries.name: What are Invocations?
entries: Beyond their choice of archetype, each class has a second level of customization collectively referred to as invocations. These invocations are as follows:

items: Berserkers have Berserker Instincts.
Consulars have Force-Empowered Casting.
Engineers have Modification Slots, which vary based on their class.
Fighters have their Combat Superiority Maneuvers.
Guardians have their Guardian Auras.
Monks have their Monastic Vows.
Operatives have their Operative Exploits.
Scholars have their Academic Superiority Maneuvers {@i and} Discoveries.
Scouts have their Scout Routines.
Sentinels have their Sentinel Ideals.

entries: Of the ten classes, only engineers (mostly), fighters, and scholars can re-choose their invocations, and even then only sparingly. Using this rule, you can instead let all ten classes re-choose their invocations, at appropriate intervals.

entries.name: When Can They Re-choose?
entries: The easiest route would be to allow characters to re-choose one of their invocation options when they complete a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}, or even when they level up. Alternatively, you might enforce a narrative moment for them to re-choose. For instance, a guardian might not be able to relearn their Guardian Aura without spending some time with their master, while a monk might have to spend time in a monastery to re-choose a Monastic Vow, and a scout might have to spend time alone practicing to re-choose a Scout Routine. Ultimately, the method in which allow your players to re-choose their invocations is up to you and your playgroup. You might even let them re-choose on the fly.

entries.name: Re-choosing Archetypes or Classes?
entries: Re-choosing archetypes or classes is not intended as a part of this variant rule. However, you could easily allow players to do so, though I'd recommend the narrative approach over the simple level up or {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}.

data.name: Longer Rests
entries: SW5e offers greater character customization than traditional 5e, and ultimately yields more powerful characters. If you find yourself struggling to challenge your party, consider using the following variant rule to make them stretch their resources.

entries.name: Quick Rest
entries: A quick rest is a period of downtime, at least 1 hour long, during which a character does nothing more strenuous than eating, drinking, reading, and tending to wounds.

A character can spend one or more Hit Dice at the end of a quick rest, up to the character's maximum number of Hit Dice, which is equal to the character's level. Whenever a character spends a Hit Die to regain {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}, the player rolls the die and adds the character's Constitution modifier to it. The character regains {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} equal to the total. The player can decide to spend an additional Hit Die after each roll.

entries.name: Short Rest
entries: A {@variantrule Short Rest|sw5e-phb|short rest} is a period of extended downtime, at least 8 hours long, during which a character sleeps for at least 6 hours and performs light activity, such as reading, talking, eating, or standing watch, for no more than 2 hours. If the rest is interrupted by a period of strenuous activity—fighting, casting powers, at least 4 hours of walking, or similar adventuring activity—the characters must restart the rest to benefit from it.

At the end of a {@variantrule Short Rest|sw5e-phb|short rest}, a character regains missing {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} up to half their hit point maximum (rounded up). A character can then spend one or more Hit Dice, up to the character's maximum number of Hit Dice, which is equal to the character's level. Whenever a character spends a Hit Die to regain {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}, the player rolls the die and adds the character's Constitution modifier to it. The character regains {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} equal to the total. The player can decide to spend an additional Hit Die after each roll.

A character can't benefit from more than one {@variantrule Short Rest|sw5e-phb|short rest} in a 24-hour period, and a character must have at least 1 hit point at the start of the rest to gain its benefits.

entries.name: Long Rest
entries: A {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest} is a period of extended downtime, at least 2 days long, during which a character sleeps for at least 6 hours each day, and performs light activity, such as reading, talking, eating, or standing watch during the remainder of the {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}. If the rest is interrupted by a period of strenuous activity—fighting, casting powers, at least 4 hours of walking, or similar adventuring activity—the characters must restart the rest to benefit from it.

At the end of a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}, a character regains all lost {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}. The character also regains spent Hit Dice, up to a number of dice equal to half of the character's total number of them (minimum of one).

A character can't benefit from more than one {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest} in a 7-day period, and a character must have at least 1 hit point at the start of the rest to gain its benefits.

entries.name: Power Durations and Other Effects
entries: Certain powers, such as {@i battle precognition} or {@i force barrier}, are powers that are intended to be cast once or twice per adventuring day. Since long rests are now once per week instead of once per day, consider increasing the duration of these powers to 24 hours, or even up to three days, as you deem appropriate.

data.name: Milestone Leveling
entries: I won't delve too far into this. The simplified version is that instead of receiving experience for every encounter and leveling up at odd times, the GM chooses when they level up. Additionally, there never has the potential to be an experience, and consequently level, disparity between players.

data.name: Overlapping Features
entries: Many species have features that make them better in certain martial ways: special traits like natural armor, armor and weapon proficiencies, or {@variantrule Unarmed Strike|sw5e-phb|unarmed strikes} and natural weapons. Counterintuitively, when those species choose certain classes, those features become obsolete instead of enhancing their class choice.
If you players choose such a species/class combination, consider using this variant rule.

entries.name: Armor Proficiencies
entries: Many species come with specific armor proficiencies suited to their species' culture, such as chiss or draethos, or natural unarmored defense, such as aing-tii or wookie. If a player chooses a species and class combination that would grant the same armor proficiencies, or a species with natural armor and a class with unarmored defense, consider instead granting them a bonus depending on the type of armor, as shown below:

items: {@b Unarmored Defense:} +1 bonus to AC while not wearing armor or wielding a {@item Shield|sw5e-phb|shield}.
{@b Light Armor:} +1 bonus to Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} while wearing {@filter light armor|items|type=light armor}.
{@b Medium Armor:} +1 bonus to Constitution {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} while wearing {@filter medium armor|items|type=medium armor}.
{@b Heavy Armor:} -1 damage taken from weapons while wearing {@filter heavy armor|items|type=heavy armor}. If this would reduce the damage to 0, the damage is instead reduced to 1.

entries: For instance, at 1st level, a draethos operative with a 16 in Dexterity would have +6 to Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} instead of +5 while wearing {@filter light armor|items|type=light armor}, while a wookiee berserker with a 14 in Dexterity and a 16 in Constitution would have an {@variantrule Armor Class|sw5e-phb} of 16 while unarmored, instead of 15. A character should only gain each bonus once.

entries.name: Weapon Proficiencies
entries: Many species come with specific weapon proficiencies suited to their species' culture, such as chiss or tuskens. If a player chooses a species and class combination that would grant the same weapon proficiencies, consider instead granting them a +1 bonus to damage rolls with the chosen weapon. For instance, at 1st level, a chiss scout with a 16 in Dexterity would have a +4 to damage rolls instead of a +3 when attacking with a {@item Blaster pistol|sw5e-phb} or {@item Sniper rifle|sw5e-phb|sniper rifle}. A character should only gain this bonus once, and this bonus does not apply if the species offers a choice of weapons, such as human or echani.

entries.name: Unarmed Strikes/Natural Weapons
entries: Many species come with higher unarmed strike damage, such as twi'lek or zabrak, or a natural weapon, such as chevin or karkarodons, representing their natural aptitude with unarmed combat. If a player chooses a species, class, or customization option combination that would both grant an increased unarmed strike, consider instead granting them a +1 bonus to their unarmed strike damage. For instance, at 1st level, a zabrak monk with a 16 in Dexterity would do 1d4+4 instead of 1d4+3 with their {@variantrule Unarmed Strike|sw5e-phb|unarmed strikes}. A character should only gain this bonus once.
Additionally, consider allowing those species that have natural weapons to use those weapons in place of their {@variantrule Unarmed Strike|sw5e-phb|unarmed strikes}, as appropriate.

entries.name: Situational Expertise
entries: Certain special traits, such as the aqualish Arms Dealer trait, give {@variantrule Expertise|sw5e-phb|expertise} in a skill in a certain situation. If you would already have {@variantrule Expertise|sw5e-phb|expertise} in that situation, instead treat this feature as if it gave {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}.

data.name: Replacing Powers
entries: Often a player might feel restricted because they made a bad power choice, and they don't want to wait until their next level up to do so. If this is a mechanic that suits your players, consider using the following variant rule.

Each time a character completes a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}, they can attempt to take one power they know and replace it with another power, as long as that power is not of a higher level than their Max Power Level. If the character knows both force and {@book tech powers|sw5e-phb|12|Tech Powers}, those powers can only be replaced with another force or {@book tech power|sw5e-phb|12|Tech Powers}, respectively.

The character immediately unlearns the power they are trying to replace, and then must make a force- or tech-casting {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} (using Wisdom or Charisma as appropriate, depending on {@book force power|sw5e-phb|11|Force Powers} alignment) with proficiency. The DC of the check varies depending on the level of the power the character is attempting to learn, as shown in the Power Level Check DC table below.

entries.name: Power Level Check DC
entries: On a success, the new power is learned. On a failure, the new power is not learned, the old power is still forgotten, and the character can't try again until their next {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}.
When attempting to replace a power, if the character currently has a vacant power known slot, they do not need to first unlearn a power before attempting to fill that slot.

data.name: Saving Throw Checks
entries: Also published in the Unearthed Arcana: Variant Rules was a rule for your players to roll when they use powers or abilities that call for a save DC. Instead of the GM making {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} against the players' static save DCs, the players roll a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} check against the GM's defense save DC.

entries.name: Calculating Saving Throw Check
entries: If players have their save throw DCs calculated, simply subtract 8 from that value. If your consular's force save DC is 15, your {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} check modifier is +7.

entries.name: Calculating Defense Save DC
entries: Monster cards also include potential {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws}, which can easily be converted to a defense save DC. Take the appropriate ability score modifier and add 14 to it. If the monster is proficient in the {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} (indicated in the {@i saving throw} line on the monster card, if it exists), instead use that value. For instance, if a B1 battle droid is forced to make a Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, its defense save DC would be 16 (14+2).

entries.name: Making the Roll
entries: Instead of the GM rolling {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} for the monsters, players make {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} checks by rolling a {@dice d20} and adding their {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} check modifier. If the roll meets or exceeds the defense save DC, the creature fails the {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}. If a character fails the the {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} check, the creature successfully saves.

If the defender would normally have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on the saving roll, you instead apply {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} to the {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} check, and vice versa if the defender would have {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage}.

data.name: Simplified Forcecasting
entries: The current version of the SW5e PHB has the player using different ability scores depending on the alignment of the powers they are trying to cast: Wisdom for light side, Charisma for dark side, player's choice for universal.
For new players, this might be too complicated. Consider letting them instead choose between using Wisdom and Charisma as their {@book forcecasting ability|sw5e-phb|10|Forcecasting Ability}.

data.name: Simplified Styles and Masteries
entries: In lieu of the fighting style and fighting mastery options available in the PHB, using this variant rule you can instead use the options present here.

entries.name: Fighting Styles
entries: Certain class features or feats offer your choice of Fighting Style. Choose from the following. You can't take a Fighting Style option more than once, even if you later get to choose again.

entries.name: Brawling
entries: You are skilled at using your weight to your {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}. You gain the following benefits:

items: You are proficient with improvised weapons.
Your unarmed strike damage increases by one step (from 1 to {@dice d4}, {@dice d4} to {@dice d6}, or {@dice d6} to {@dice d8}).

When you attempt to shove or grapple a creature, or make an attack against a creature with an unarmed strike or an improvised weapon wielded in one hand on your turn, you can use your {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} to make an additional attack, grapple, or shove against the same creature.

entries.name: Close Quarters Shooting
entries: You are skilled at getting up close and personal with {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapons. While you are wielding a {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapon with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: When making a ranged {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|weapon attack} while you are within 5 feet of a hostile creature, you do not have {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on the {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}.
Your ranged weapon attacks ignore {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|half cover} against targets within 15 feet of you.
You gain a +1 bonus to {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack rolls} you make with {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapons.

entries.name: Defense
entries: You are skilled at the art of defending yourself. While you are wearing armor with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: You gain a +1 bonus to AC.
You have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability checks} and {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throws} to avoid being moved.

entries.name: Dueling
entries: You are skilled in the art of fighting with a single melee weapon. While you are wielding a melee weapon in one hand with which you are proficient and no other weapons, you gain a +2 bonus to damage rolls.

entries.name: Equilibrium
entries: You are skilled at fighting while minimally armored. While you are wearing no armor and not wielding a medium or heavy {@item Shield|sw5e-phb|shield}, you gain the following benefits:

items: You gain a +1 bonus to AC.
You gain a +1 bonus to {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack rolls} you make with {@variantrule Unarmed Strike|sw5e-phb|unarmed strikes} and weapon attacks.

entries.name: Great Weapon Fighting
entries: You are skilled at putting the weight of a weapon to your {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}. While you are wielding a melee weapon in two hands with which you are proficient, when you roll a 1 or 2 on a damage die for an attack, you can reroll the die and must use the new roll, even if the new roll is a 1 or a 2.

entries.name: Sentinel
entries: You are skilled at techniques that take {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} of every drop in any enemy's guard. While you are wielding a melee weapon with which you are proficient, you can use a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} to enter a defensive stance that lasts until the start of your next turn. While in your defensive stance, you can make a number of {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attacks} equal to your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} without using your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb}, and you can use your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to make a melee attack against a creature that moves more than 5 feet while within your reach.

entries.name: Sharpshooting
entries: You are skilled with {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapons and can make shots that others find difficult. While you are wielding a {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapon with which you are proficient, gain a +2 bonus to ranged weapon attacks.

entries.name: Shielding
entries: You are skilled at using your {@item Shield|sw5e-phb|shield} to defend your allies as well as yourself. While you are wielding a {@item Shield|sw5e-phb|shield} with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: When a creature you can see attacks a target other than you that is within 5 feet of you, you can use your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to impose {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on the {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}.
If you are wielding a heavy {@item Shield|sw5e-phb|shield}, you are no longer required to wield a weapon with the light property in the other hand.

entries.name: Throwing
entries: You are skilled with the techniques of throwing weapons. While you are wielding a weapon with the thrown property with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: You gain a +1 bonus to ranged attack and damage rolls.
Whenever you make a ranged attack with a thrown weapon, you can immediately draw another weapon as part of the attack.

entries.name: Two-Weapon Fighting
entries: You are skilled at fighting with two weapons. While you are wielding separate weapons in each hand, or a weapon with the double property, with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: When you engage in Two-Weapon Fighting, you can add your ability modifier to the damage of your Two-Weapon Fighting attack.
When you make an {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attack}, you can attack with both of your weapons.

entries.name: Versatile Fighting
entries: You are skilled at using weapons in different ways. While you are wielding a melee weapon with the versatile property with which you are proficient and no other weapons, you gain the following benefits:

items: You gain a +1 bonus to {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack rolls} while wielding a weapon in one hand.
You gain a +1 bonus to damage rolls while wielding a weapon in two hands.

entries.name: Fighting Masteries
entries: Certain class features or feats offer your choice of Fighting Mastery. Choose from the following. You can't take a Fighting Mastery option more than once, even if you later get to choose again.

entries.name: Brawling Mastery
entries: You've mastered using your weight to your {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}, easily wrangling targets around. You gain the following benefits:

items: Your improvised weapons use a {@dice d6} for damage and gain the versatile (2d4) property.
Your unarmed strike damage increases by one step (from 1 to {@dice d4}, {@dice d4} to {@dice d6}, or {@dice d6} to {@dice d8}).
Your {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} isn't halved by carrying a {@condition Grappled|sw5e-phb|grappled} creature who is the same size category as you or smaller.

Once per turn, when you hit a creature with an unarmed strike or an improvised weapon, you can make an additional unarmed strike or improvised {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|weapon attack} against the same target without the aid of your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} (no action required).

entries.name: Close Quarters Shooting Mastery
entries: You've mastered getting up close and personal with {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapons, maintain both rate of fire and accuracy. While you are wielding a {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapon with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: When you take the {@action Attack|sw5e-phb} action, you can choose to fire rapidly at the expense of accuracy. Your ranged weapon attacks are made without the aid of your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}, but you use your {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} to make an additional ranged {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|weapon attack}, also without your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}.
Your ranged weapon attacks ignore {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|half cover} against targets within 30 feet of you.

Other creatures provoke an {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attack} from you when they move to within 15 feet of you, and you can use {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapons when making {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attacks}.

entries.name: Defense Mastery
entries: You've mastered the art of defending yourself, treating your armor as a second skin. While you are wearing armor with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: Critical hits made against you are treated as normal hits.
When a creature makes a melee attack against you and misses, you can use your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to attempt to shove that creature up to 10 feet directly away from you.

entries.name: Dueling Mastery
entries: Your mastery of fighting with a single melee weapon is unsurpassed; you make one weapon feel like many. While you are wielding a melee weapon in one hand with which you are proficient and no other weapons, you gain the following benefits:

items: When you take the {@action Attack|sw5e-phb} action, you can decide to attack with haste at the expense of accuracy. Your melee weapon attacks are made without the aid of your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}, but you use your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to make an additional {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|melee weapon attack}, also without your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}.

When a creature hits you with a melee attack, you can use your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to add your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} to your AC for that attack, potentially causing the attack to miss you.

entries.name: Great Weapon Mastery
entries: You've mastered putting the weight of a weapon to your {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage}, letting its momentum empower your strikes. While you are wielding a melee weapon in two hands with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: On your turn, when you score a {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit} with a melee weapon or reduce a creature to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} with one, you can make one {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|melee weapon attack} as a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb}.

Before you make a melee attack with a weapon that you are wielding in two-hands with which you are proficient with, you can choose to forgo your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}. If the attack hits, you add double your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} to the attack's damage.

entries.name: Sentinel Mastery
entries: You've mastered techniques to take {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} of every drop in any enemy's guard; in tight spaces you are indomitable. While you are wielding a melee weapon with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: When you hit a creature with an {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attack}, the creature's {@variantrule Speed|sw5e-phb|speed} becomes 0 for the rest of the turn.
Creatures within 5 feet of you provoke {@action Opportunity Attack|sw5e-phb|opportunity attacks} from you even if they take the {@action Disengage|sw5e-phb} action before leaving your reach.

entries.name: Sharpshooting Mastery
entries: You have mastered {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapons and can easily make shots that others find impossible. While you are wielding a {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapon with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: Attacking at long range doesn't impose {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on your ranged {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|weapon attack rolls}.
Your ranged weapon attacks ignore {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|half cover} and three-quarters {@variantrule Cover|sw5e-phb|cover}.

Before you make an attack with a {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} weapon that you are proficient with, you can choose to forgo your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}. If the attack hits, you add double your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} to the attack's damage.

entries.name: Shielding Mastery
entries: You've mastered using a {@item Shield|sw5e-phb|shield} to defend your allies as well as yourself, and you understand that {@item Shield|sw5e-phb|shields} are not just for protection but also for offense. While you are wielding a {@item Shield|sw5e-phb|shield} with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: If you take the {@action Attack|sw5e-phb} action on your turn, you can use a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb} to try to shove a creature within 5 feet of you with your {@item Shield|sw5e-phb|shield}.

If you aren't {@condition Incapacitated|sw5e-phb|incapacitated}, you can add your {@item Shield|sw5e-phb|shield}'s AC bonus to any Dexterity {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} you make against a power or other harmful effect.

entries.name: Throwing Mastery
entries: You've mastered the techniques of throwing weapons, readily blending the weapons with your movements. While you are wielding a weapon with the thrown property with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: You gain a +1 bonus to ranged {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack rolls} you make with thrown weapons.
Attacking at long range doesn't impose {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on your ranged {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|weapon attack rolls} with thrown weapons.

When you hit a creature with a ranged {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|weapon attack} with a thrown weapon, you have {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on your next {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|melee weapon attack} against that creature before the end of your next turn.
You can use Two-Weapon Fighting even when the melee weapons you are wielding in one hand aren't light, if at least one of them has the thrown property.

entries.name: Two-Weapon Mastery
entries: You've mastered fighting with two weapons, becoming a flurry of motion. While you are wielding separate weapons in each hand, or a weapon with the double property, with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: While wielding separate weapons in each hand, you gain a +1 bonus to AC.
While wielding a double weapon, when you roll a 1 on a weapon damage die, you can reroll the die and must use the new roll, even if the new roll is a 1.
You can engage in Two-Weapon Fighting even when the weapons you are wielding lack the light property.
You can draw or stow two weapons when you would normally be able to draw or stow only one.

When you engage in Two-Weapon Fighting, you can choose to forgo your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}. If you do so, you can make an additional Two-Weapon Fighting attack, also without your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}.

entries.name: Versatile Mastery
entries: You've mastered the art of using weapons in different ways, altering your attack patterns mid-swing. While you are wielding a melee weapon with the versatile property with which you are proficient and no other weapons, you gain the following benefits:

items: When you are the target of a {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|melee weapon attack}, you can immediately use your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to make a {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|melee weapon attack} against the target without your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}. On a hit, you impose {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on the {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} made against you.

If you miss an attack while wielding a weapon in two hands, you can immediately make an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll} against the same target using one hand. You can only make this attack once per turn. If the two-handed attack was made with {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} or without your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}, this attack is made the same way.

If you miss an attack while wielding a weapon in one hand, you can immediately attempt to shove that creature up to 5 feet directly away from you. You can only make this attempt once per turn. If the one-handed attack was made with {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} or without your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}, this {@variantrule Ability Check|sw5e-phb|ability check} is made the same way.

data.name: Starship Destiny
entries: SSometimes a starship is more than just a means of transportation. Sometimes, it's part of a character's destiny. In fact, for some characters, it's the focal point of their destiny, which might otherwise be nothing more than to wander aimlessly from one jam to another. No matter how humble (or downright ramschackle) a starship might appear, if it's the destiny of a character to be linked with that ship, it can accomplish amazing things.

If you decide to link a starship (or, rarely, a planetary vehicle) to your destiny, that replaces the normal destiny mechanic. In essence, you don't have a destiny to accomplish any specific goal; instead, you're destined have the most important events in your life with a specific starship. This option is appropriate in campaigns with at least a moderate frequency of starship-scale encounters, but it's certainly not restricted to such campaigns. In fact, if a campaign centers exclusively around starship-scale action, this option might be too powerful as it allows access to Destiny Points in most encounters. Only the GM can decide if starship-linked destinies are appropriate for a given campaign.

You earn and spend Destiny Points with a starship-linked destiny using the same basic rules as with the normal destiny options. However, having your destiny linked to a starship causes the rules to work slightly differently.
Firstly, Destiny Points are earned when you experience (and survive) key campaign events involving you and your starship.

Secondly, if a starship is your destiny, it is never completely destroyed. Even if it is blown up in battle or confiscated by Hutts before being crushed and melted, some small part of it survives. Perhaps you find the hyperspace core the whole starship was built around, or its ruined hull is found drifting as debris after that battle. Your starship can cease to be functional as easily as anyone else's, but a recognizable part of it always survives for you to rebuild (or retrofit to a similar starship). It can be as time consuming and difficult as getting a new starship would be (if not more so), but the result still qualifies as your destiny-linked starship.

Finally, the options you can exercise by using a Destiny Point are slightly different, as detailed below. The following are possible only when you are acting as a crew member (pilot, gunner, mechanic, operator or coordinator) on the starship linked to your destiny:

items: Cause an attack rolled against your starship to suffer {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage}, or gain {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on a {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} against an attack on your starship, even once the attack is resolved. (Coordinator or pilot)
Gain {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on any pilot check. (Pilot)
Allow your starship to act out of turn, thus changing your position in the {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} order. (Coordinator, operator, or pilot)

Gain {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on an {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack roll}, or impose {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on an enemy {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, against an attack from your ship's weapons. (Coordinator, gunner, or operator)
Repair your starship, restoring {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} by rolling a number of its hit die equal to or less than your level. (Mechanic)
Immediately restore your starship's {@item Shield|sw5e-phb|shields} to full. (Mechanic or operator)
Gain {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on any skill check made to interact with the ship.
Immediately gain 2 tactical dice.

entries: In general, a character with a starship-linked destiny can do what no one else can manage - unless they, too, are linked to its destiny. There's nothing to prevent multiple characters from being destiny-linked to the same starship. Such characters might share the ship, or might constantly be stealing, buying or gambling it back and forther between them.

data.name: Strenuous Combat
entries: Combat is a stressful activity, both physically and mentally. If you want to add an additional layer to combat to help encourage your players to handle things in a more civilized manner, consider implementing this variant rule.

entries.name: Concluding Combat
entries: At the end of a combat encounter, you might consider having each surviving participant make a Constitution {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} to avoid {@condition Exhaustion|sw5e-phb|exhaustion}. The DC for the {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} is equal to 10 + the number of complete rounds that occurred during the encounter. On a failure, a creature suffers 1 level of {@condition Exhaustion|sw5e-phb|exhaustion}.

entries.name: More Restful Rest
entries: {@condition Exhaustion|sw5e-phb} is a painful penalty to add to characters, especially if they end up encountering multiple levels of {@condition Exhaustion|sw5e-phb|exhaustion} over the course of a gaming day. When your players' characters complete a {@variantrule Short Rest|sw5e-phb|short rest} with {@condition Exhaustion|sw5e-phb|exhaustion} from this variant, consider allowing them to spend a Hit Die at the end of that rest to remove one level of {@condition Exhaustion|sw5e-phb|exhaustion}.

If a character encounters multiple levels of {@condition Exhaustion|sw5e-phb|exhaustion} due to this variant, they can spend more Hit Dice to remove the additional levels, either during the same rest or separate ones. Each time they do so, however, the effect is cumulative for each additional level. Removing a second level of {@condition Exhaustion|sw5e-phb|exhaustion} would take two Hit Dice, while a third would take three, and so on. For instance, if a character completes a {@variantrule Short Rest|sw5e-phb|short rest} with two levels of {@condition Exhaustion|sw5e-phb|exhaustion} from this variant, they could spend one Hit Die to remove one level of {@condition Exhaustion|sw5e-phb|exhaustion}, or three Hit Dice to remove both. Once a creature has completed a {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest}, the number of Hit Dice to be spent to remove this {@condition Exhaustion|sw5e-phb|exhaustion} is reduced back to one.

data.name: Tactical Initiative
entries: Rather than each player character and creature acting on their own, two or more allied creatures can instead choose to act tactically and work together using this {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} variant rule.

entries.name: Rolling Tactical Initiative
entries: When combat begins and {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} would be rolled, two or more allied creatures can choose to work as a unit, provided they can see or hear and understand each other. When they do so, they each roll {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} separately, adding any modifiers as appropriate. Once each individual party has rolled their {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative}, the group then acts using the lowest result. Once a tactical group is formed, each character's {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} is set to the lowest result, even if the tactical group separates.

For instance, if three players want to use tactical {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative}, and they roll a 17, an 11, and a 14, all three players will instead act on {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} 11.

entries.name: Multiple Tactical Groups
entries: The party can use multiple tactical groups rather than all working in concert. For instance, a party of five might split into a tactical group of three and a tactical group of two, each group rolling their tactical {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} separately. A character can only belong to one tactical group at a time.

entries.name: Acting in Concert
entries: When a tactical group's turn comes up in the {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} order, each member of the group acts together. Their turns and actions can come in any order, though each individual tactical group member is still limited to what actions they could normally take. Additionally, actions that could normally be broken up, such as when a fighter takes the {@action Attack|sw5e-phb} action and has the Extra Attack feature, can be broken up during the turn.

For instance, a 5th-level fighter might take the {@action Attack|sw5e-phb} action and make their first attack. Before they make their second attack, however, the operative ally in their tactical group might then take the {@action Help|sw5e-phb} action to grant them {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} before the fighter makes the second attack.

entries.name: Separating a Tactical Group
entries: When a tactical group loses contact with each other, or if the tactical group chooses to break up on their turn (no action required), the tactical group becomes separated. When separated, each member of the former tactical group acts on their own, though they retain the {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} of the tactical group. The order of any active members of the former tactical group acting on the same {@variantrule Initiative|sw5e-phb|initiative} is determined randomly.

data.name: Weapon Sundering
entries: YYou can attempt to damage, and potentially destroy, a weapon held by a hostile creature. On your turn, you can take the Sundering action to damage an enemy's weapon. Make a {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|melee weapon attack} roll with {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} against the target's {@variantrule Armor Class|sw5e-phb} as normal. If the attack hits, roll weapon damage and instead apply the damage to one weapon being wielded by your target.

entries.name: Weapon Hit Dice and Hit Points
entries: A weapon's {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} are presented both as Hit Dice and {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}. A weapon has a number of Hit Dice equal to twice its damage dice. For instance, a {@item Blaster rifle|sw5e-phb} has a 1d8 damage die, so it has 2 Hit Dice, which are d8s. A weapon's {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} are determined by taking the average of its hit dice. For instance, a {@filter blaster|items|firearm=true} has 2 Hit Dice, which are d8s, so it has 9 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} on average, as shown in the Hit Dice Average table below.

entries.name: Hit Dice Average

colLabels: Average {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb} per Hit Die

entries: At the GM's discretion, some weapons might be resistant, immune, or even vulnerable to certain types of damage. Enhanced weapons are resistance, or even immune, to damage from unenhanced weapons.

entries.name: Repairing Damaged/Broken Weapons
entries: A weapon is destroyed when it drops to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}. As long as a weapon has 1 or more {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} remaining, a character can attempt to perform minor repairs by spending one or more of the weapon's Hit Dice at the end of a {@variantrule Short Rest|sw5e-phb|short rest}, up to the weapon's maximum number of Hit Dice. To restore hit dice, the player must first make an Intelligence ({@skill Technology|sw5e-phb}) check If a weapon has at least 1 HP remaining, you can attempt to make minor repairs to it during a {@variantrule Short Rest|sw5e-phb}. To attempt to restore HD, a character must make an Intelligence ({@skill Technology|sw5e-phb}) roll. The DC is 8 + the amount of damage the weapon has taken. The player has {@variantrule Advantage|sw5e-phb|advantage} on the roll if they know the {@i mending} {@book tech power|sw5e-phb|12|Tech Powers} or are proficient with the appropriate artisan's tools (armstech's tools for {@filter blasters|items|firearm=true} and {@filter vibroweapons|items|type=martial weapon}, artificer's tools for {@filter lightweapons|items|type=martial weapon|category=lightweapon}). On a failure, the Hit Die is expended and no {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} are restored. On a success, the player can spend the weapon's Hit Dice to restore {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}. The player can decide to spend an additional Hit Die after each roll.

A weapon regains Hit Dice when serviced by a professional with the appropriate artisan's tools, who can repair the weapon over a number of hours equal to the size of the weapon's damage dice. For instance, a {@item Blaster rifle|sw5e-phb} has a 1d8 damage die, so it would take 8 hours to repair. This service costs half the value of the weapon.

In reality, {@filter lightweapons|items|type=martial weapon|category=lightweapon} are probably more effective than {@filter vibroweapons|items|type=martial weapon} when it comes to sundering weapons. For the sake of balance, they aren't. At the GM's discretion, weapons might be resistant to kinetic damage, or vulnerable to energy damage, to represent this effectiveness.
A player can choose to specialize their character with the following features.

entries.name: Fighting Style
entries: Certain class features or feats offer your choice of Fighting Style. As a part of this variant rule, you should allow your players to take the following Fighting Style instead of the options listed in the Player Handbook. You can't take a Fighting Style option more than once, even if you later get to choose again.

entries.name: Sunder Fighting
entries: You are skilled at striking in order to damage, and potentially destroy, your enemies' weapons. While you are wielding a melee weapon with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: You no longer have {@variantrule Disadvantage|sw5e-phb|disadvantage} on Sundering {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|attack rolls}.

When a foe hits you with a Sundering attack, you can use your {@variantrule Reaction|sw5e-phb} to add a +5 to your {@variantrule Armor Class|sw5e-phb|armor class} vs the triggering attack. If this causes the attack to miss, your weapon does not take any damage.

entries.name: Fighting Mastery
entries: A feat represents a talent or an area of {@variantrule Expertise|sw5e-phb|expertise} that gives character special capabilities. It embodies training, experience, and abilities beyond what a class provides. At certain levels, your class gives you the Ability Score Improvement feature. Using the optional feats rule, you can forgo taking that feature to take a feat of your choice instead. You can take each feat only once, unless the feat's description says otherwise. As a part of this variant rule, you should allow your players to take the following feat instead of the options listed in the Player Handbook.

entries.name: Sundering Mastery
entries: You have mastered rending your foes' weapons, leaving them impotent and vulnerable to your follow up attacks. While you are wielding a melee weapon with which you are proficient, you gain the following benefits:

items: Before you make a Sundering attack with weapon that you are proficient with, you can choose to forgo your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus}. If the attack hits, you add double your {@variantrule Proficiency|sw5e-phb|Proficiency Bonus} to the attack's damage.

On your turn, when you score a {@variantrule Critical Hit|sw5e-phb|critical hit} with a Sundering attack or reduce a weapon to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} with one, you can make one {@variantrule Attack Roll|sw5e-phb|melee weapon attack} as a {@variantrule Bonus Action|sw5e-phb}.

data.name: Wounds
entries: When a character is reduced to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}, begins making {@variantrule Death Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|death saving throws}, and has {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} restored, they can return to the battle no worse for the wear. Using this variant rule, you can add an additional layer to make falling to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} more threatening.

entries.name: Gaining Wounds
entries: When a character is reduced to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points}, that character must make a DC 10 Constitution {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}. On a success, nothing happens, but the DC of this {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw} for that character increases by 5, cumulatively, until they complete a short or {@variantrule Long Rest|sw5e-phb|long rest} or fail the {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, at which point the DC resets to 10. On a failed save, the character suffers 1 wounded level. On a success or a failure, a creature immediately gains one {@variantrule Death Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|death saving throw} failure for each wounded level it has.

For instance, if a character with no wounded levels is reduced to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} and fails their Constitution {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, they gain 1 wounded level, and they then gain 1 {@variantrule Death Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|death saving throw} failure for their 1 wounded level. Alternatively, if a character with 2 wounded levels is reduced to 0 {@variantrule Hit Points|sw5e-phb|hit points} and succeeds on their Constitution {@variantrule Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|saving throw}, they don't gain a wounded level, but they then gain 2 {@variantrule Death Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|death saving throw} failures for their 2 wounded levels. If they take damage, or fail the {@variantrule Death Saving Throw|sw5e-phb|death saving throw} they make at the start of their next turn, they immediately die.

entries.name: Clearing Wounds
entries: A character loses all wounded levels when they are restored to their hit point maximum, whether through consumables, powers, resting, or other means.
